clue.text: Unwell, in pain, nurses finally treat leg and part of foot

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: an ache is a pain

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of nurses
to tend a wound is to treat it
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side
to be unwell is to be ill

explanation.surface: A sick patient in pain has nurses who finally see to a leg and foot.
explanation.walkthrough: ILL sits inside ACHE to give ACHILLE. In cricket, the leg side of the field is the on side, so leg = ON is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: The big tendon joining the calf muscle to the heel bone runs down the back of the foot.

clue.text: Find name in Yell for somewhere selling wicked products

indicators.note: to find one thing in another is to see it sitting inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: to cry out is to yell
a handle is a name, especially a nickname or username

explanation.surface: Looking someone up in Yell, the business directory, to find a shop selling sinful goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Yell is the UK's old Yellow Pages directory, which makes the surface feel like a phone-book search. 'Wicked' means having a wick, not being evil.
explanation.definitionFit: A chandler originally made and sold candles, and candles are the products with wicks, so a chandlery sells wicked goods.

clue.text: Playwright and poet initially leaves Bury

indicators.note: whatever leaves goes away, so those letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: Harold Pinter, the English playwright

indicators.note: initially points to the start of the word, so only its opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of poet

explanation.surface: A playwright and a poet head off and quit the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury looks like the town near Manchester, capitalised to disguise the verb. Taking the P from PINTER leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter a body is to put it in a grave, which is exactly what burying means.

clue.text: Take real pride, training to become oral transliterator

indicators.note: training shapes and reshapes something, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to a student to feel proud of their training as they qualify as an interpreter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is an instruction to the solver: take these letters, rearrange them, and they become the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who follows speech by watching mouth movements turns what is spoken into understood words, a playful description of that skill.

clue.text: Two packs of aggregate including small credit

indicators.note: a thing that includes another holds it within itself, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a sum is an aggregate total
CR is the short form of credit in accounts

explanation.surface: Two bags of gravel or building aggregate, with a small amount of credit included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Packs' reads like bags of builders' aggregate; in rugby the pack is a team's forwards. 'Small' tells you to abbreviate credit.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby a scrum is formed when the two teams' forwards bind together and push against each other.

clue.text: Training worries

definitions.meaning: first meaning: drills or workouts done for practice
second meaning: troubles someone, as in being exercised about a problem

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a noun phrase about training anxiety, but the two words are separate meanings of one word, the second a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Workouts done for practice are one sense; the other is the verb for troubling someone's mind, as when an issue preoccupies a person.

clue.text: Padre dressed in shroud

indicators.note: to dress something is to arrange or prepare it, so these letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chaplain wrapped in a burial cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed' fits the picture of vestments, which hides its role as the signal to rearrange the priest's title.
explanation.definitionFit: To shroud something is to cover or wrap it in cloth, which is what draping it does.

clue.text: Grandmother eager to produce clothing

parts.note: nan is an informal word for grandmother
to be keen is to be eager

explanation.surface: Granny can't wait to make some clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests knitting; the answer is a fabric, and trousers made of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowish cotton cloth from China, originally from Nanjing; garments made from it, especially trousers, were called by the same name.

clue.text: High Street shops — they need the dough, we're told

parts.note: first meaning: shops selling bread and cakes
second meaning: the people who work dough by hand, once the verb is heard correctly

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: need sounds the same as knead, to work dough with the hands

explanation.surface: Town-centre shops are struggling and need money to survive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We're told' says to hear 'need' as 'knead'. Dough is also slang for money, which makes the shops seem short of cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Shops selling bread are named for their workers, and those workers work dough by hand before baking it.

clue.text: A normal time to get divorced

parts.note: taken as written
par is the normal or expected level
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone wondering when the usual moment is to end a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: PAR is the golf score an expert is expected to make, hence normal, as in 'par for the course'.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple who have divorced are separated, living their lives away from each other.

clue.text: China police ran amok

indicators.note: running amok is running wild and out of control, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Riot police went on the rampage in China.
explanation.walkthrough: China is capitalised as the country, but it is the crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: China is fine ceramic tableware, and porcelain is the material it is made of, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Back final runner at 'untingdon?

parts.note: the final part is the end
a runner at a racecourse is a horse; dropping the H, as in 'untingdon, gives it without its first letter

explanation.surface: A punter backing the last horse in a race at Huntingdon.
explanation.walkthrough: Huntingdon has a racecourse, so a runner there is a horse; the apostrophe copies the dropped H of Cockney speech, telling you to drop it from horse too.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a plan or candidate is to give it support and approval, which is the meaning of the answer.

clue.text: Friend in possession of revolutionary weapon

indicators.note: to possess something is to hold it, so one word holds the other

parts.note: a mate is a friend
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: A comrade found holding a rebel's gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Che Guevara is the stock crossword revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad heavy blade used for cutting vegetation, which can also be wielded in a fight.

clue.text: Clear scope for a glove puppet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to brush a floor or area clean
second meaning: the range or extent of something
third meaning: the grey dog puppet who partnered Sooty on British children's television

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings, not two: Sweep is the squeaking dog glove puppet from the British children's show Sooty.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for brushing clean, a noun for range or extent, and as the name of Sooty's dog friend.

clue.text: Being talented, I burst into song at the end of concert

indicators.note: placing something at the end of another sets it right after, so the pieces go in that order

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms
taken as written
to burst into song is to start to sing

explanation.surface: A gifted performer bursts into song at the close of a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are the BBC's summer season of concerts in London; PROM is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing talent means showing signs of future success, the loose adjectival sense of the answer, as in a promising young player.

clue.text: Outfit with feathers gets reprimand

parts.note: a dress is an outfit
down is soft fine feathers

explanation.surface: Someone wearing a feathered costume is told off for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the feathers on the outfit; in the answer they are two separate pieces, the second being soft plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a dressing-down is to scold them severely, so the phrasal verb means to tell off.

clue.text: Segregate variety of chocolate

indicators.note: a variety is a different version of something, so these letters come in a different form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sorting chocolates into their different kinds.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the answer is one kind of chocolate, not a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The egg-shaped confection given at the spring festival is usually made of chocolate, so it is an example of it.

clue.text: Former teacher produces great painting

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a schoolmaster from the past
second meaning: a work by a leading European painter before about 1800

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a retired art teacher painting a masterpiece, but the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolmaster of old is one sense; the other is the art-world term for a distinguished pre-modern European artist or one of their works.

clue.text: Derby and Oaks arrange equipment for reporters?

indicators.note: to arrange things is to set them in a new order, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Organisers of two famous horse races set up the press facilities.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby and the Oaks are classic English flat races run at Epsom. The question mark admits the definition is loose: reporters type on these.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists write their copy by typing, so the sets of keys on their computers are their basic working equipment.

clue.text: King raises problem with German leaders

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: a problem is something gone wrong, so these letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch brings up a difficulty with the heads of Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raises problem' reads as bringing up an issue; 'problem' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaiser was the title of the German emperors, so the plural names the country's former rulers.

clue.text: South of France linked to a North African country

parts.note: sud is French for south
an is another form of the article a

explanation.surface: The south of France has connections with a country in North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South of France' looks like the region, but it means the French word for south.
explanation.definitionFit: The republic lying south of Egypt on the Nile is a North African state.

clue.text: Hundred up with openers from Birmingham and Durham in reasonable form

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a ton is a hundred, as in a century of runs

indicators.note: openers are the ones who start, so only the first letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the first letters of Birmingham, and, Durham

explanation.surface: A cricket scoreboard: a batsman reaches a hundred, with the opening batsmen of two county sides in good form.
explanation.walkthrough: The openers are the first letters of all three words, including 'and'. Birmingham is home to Warwickshire's ground and Durham is a county side, supporting the cricket picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying things are fairly good, as in replying to 'how are you?', describes someone or something in decent condition.

clue.text: Evening out in club on endless binge

indicators.note: something endless has no ends, so the letters at both extremes are cut away

parts.note: an iron is a golf club
binge with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A night out at a nightclub on a non-stop drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evening out' looks like a night on the town, but it means making something even. 'Endless' here trims both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing clothes with a hot iron smooths the creases, making the fabric flat and level.

clue.text: Franco-Prussian agreement on board?

definitions.note: the answer names a kind of board, completing the phrase with it

parts.note: oui is French for yes
ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A treaty between France and Prussia, agreed by the board.
explanation.walkthrough: The Franco-Prussian War suggests a treaty; really it is 'yes' in French followed by 'yes' in German, which is where the name comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The spirit-summoning board with letters and a pointer is known by this trademark, formed from French and German words of assent.

clue.text: Defend media outlet that drops The Scotsman?

indicators.note: whatever is dropped is let go and left out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: The Guardian, the British newspaper
Ian is a typically Scottish first name, the crossword's stock Scotsman

explanation.surface: Standing up for a newspaper that stops carrying its rival, The Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scotsman is set in italics as the Edinburgh newspaper, but it stands for IAN. The Guardian is a UK national daily.
explanation.definitionFit: To guard something is to protect it from harm or attack, which is what defending it means.

clue.text: Tasteful short lament by soldier

indicators.note: something cut short lacks its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: an elegy is a lament, here missing its last letter
a soldier ant is a worker type, so ant = soldier

explanation.surface: A brief, refined poem of mourning written by a serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldier = ANT is a crossword convention, from the soldier caste of ants.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tasteful shows refined judgement and style, which is what graceful, stylish things are.

clue.text: Identical time in race?

parts.note: even means equal or identical
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Runners clocking exactly the same time in a race: a dead heat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a race is only one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: At an athletics meeting each competition, such as the hundred metres, is one item on the programme.

clue.text: Get rid of main changes in aristocracy

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: the elite are the aristocracy, the top tier of society

indicators.note: something that changes takes a different form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Abolishing the chief reforms made among the nobility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main changes' reads as major reforms; 'changes' is the anagram signal acting on MAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate something is to remove or do away with it completely.

clue.text: Another old craft makes a comeback

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: making a comeback means coming back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a craft is an art or skill

explanation.surface: One more traditional handicraft is enjoying a revival.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the craft goes backwards; the old stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra one is an additional one, over and above the rest, as in asking for one more.

clue.text: Dishevelled rogues join Conservative for a laugh

parts.note: shaggy means untidy and unkempt
a dog is an old word for a rascal or rogue
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Scruffy rascals sign up with the Tory party just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The word breaks in the answer do not match the pieces: the S of the rogues begins the last word. Dog is an old word for a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A long rambling joke with a deliberately pointless punchline is told to raise a laugh, however groan-worthy.
